To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fate of a cell is determined by its cytoplasmic content and that the cytoplasmic information is not distributed evenly to all cells of the embryo.

the development of Drosophila is mosaic in the sense that (1) the fate of a cell and the fate of its descendants are determined by the genotype of the nucleus, (2) the genotype of the cytoplasm is not involved in determination, and (3) the genotype of an egg cell determines the fate of its progeny, irrespective of the genotype of the sperm cell that contributed the nucleus.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Drosophila system has been used in the past to study the role of the cytoplasm in the determination of cell fate, the role of the genome in the determination of developmental pathways, the role of gene activity in the differentiation process, the role of cell-cell interaction in morphogenetic processes, and the role of cell death in the regulation of cell numbers.
the Drosophila mosaic system has proved its usefulness in the investigation of the problem of determination, and that it will continue to do so in the future.
the genetic and developmental properties of the Drosophila genome are such that the genetic mosaic technique is an extremely useful tool for the analysis of cellular differentiation in this organism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic and developmental analysis of Drosophila chimaeras has revealed the existence of a variety of mechanisms by which the genetic constitution of a cell can influence the developmental fate of that cell and its progeny, and by which the developmental state of a cell can determine the expression of its genetic potential.
Drosophia chimeras can be produced in which the fate of a single cell or of a small group of cells can be followed during the whole period of development.

the Drosophila embryo, larva, and pupa are mosaic structures composed of cells that are genetically different from one another and that the developmental fate of these cells is determined in a manner dependent on their position in the body.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the genetic information for a particular phenotype is not necessarily confined to the nucleus of a cell but may be stored in the cytoplasm as well, and that this information can be transmitted from cell to cell.
the Drosophila embryo is an excellent experimental system for the study of the mechanisms underlying the establishment of cell lineage and the regulation of differentiation.
the Drosophila embryo and larva is a mosaic of cells that differ in genotype.
